19876-on-the-fringe-of-the-great-fight:
George Gallie Nasmith wrote On the Fringe of the Great Fight about Canadian war service. It preserves the poem In Flanders Fields within its pages. John McCrae's lines speak for the dead of Ypres. The larks still sing above the guns in that poem. The torch passes from failing hands to the living. Nasmith, a bacteriologist, served with Canadian forces in France.

A scientist at war notices water, disease, and sanitation. Nasmith's fringe is the medical and laboratory edge of battle. His memoir balances that work against famous verse. Canadian war writing is rich in such professional views. The book records how expertise served the front. It also helped fix McCrae's poem in national memory.
20395-the-story-of-the-2-4th-oxfordshire:
Captain G. K. Rose wrote the story of the 2/4th Oxfordshire and Buckinghamshire Light Infantry and its service in the First World War. The book grew from a series of articles printed in the Oxford Times during the summer of 1919. The newspaper helped the project from the start.

Battalion histories like this one record marches, trenches, and battles as the men lived them. They name the places and honour the soldiers who did not come home. For families in Oxfordshire and Buckinghamshire, such a book kept the battalion's war from fading out of memory.
21706-twice-bought:
Gold fever drives this Ballantyne tale, set beside the swift streams that run down from the Rocky Mountains to the Oregon goldfields. Tom Brixton digs hard all day, then gambles away his gains at night in Lantry's store. A big cheat named Gashford wins all Tom owns, down to his last bag of gold nuggets.

Tom's friend Fred Westly argues that honesty is the best policy, but Tom plans to steal his own gold back. Their clash over right and wrong carries the story, with drink, greed, and pride making each choice harder. Ballantyne uses the gold camp to test what a young man will do when fortune seems one throw away.
22430-evolution-in-modern-thought:
Evolution in Modern Thought gathers essays on Darwin's idea and its reach. One passage grants that Darwin did not originate evolution itself. The idea, in rough form, reaches back to Aristotle himself.

Present-day forms descend from somewhat simpler ancestors, the writer argues. Those ancestors descend from yet simpler forms in turn. The chain runs back toward literal Protozoa and Protophyta. About those first forms, he admits, we know nothing at all. Essays like these carried evolution into history, mind, and society. The volume shows educated readers digesting Darwin two generations on. It remains a clear record of an idea remaking every field it touched.
22619-international-copyright:
International Copyright is a work of argument about authors' rights across borders, treated through ethics and political economy. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. In its century, foreign publishers could often reprint a book without paying its writer, and reformers fought to end the practice by treaty.

The sample lays foundations in economic science, defining it as the ordering of men's relations in labor and in property, the fruit of labor. From that base the writer builds toward copyright as a property question with moral weight. The book belongs to the long campaign that produced modern copyright treaties. Legal historians and publishing scholars will find in it the period's own reasoning, stated in full.
22727-the-land-of-the-long-night:
Paul Du Chaillu wrote The Land of the Long Night, an 1899 travel adventure through winter Scandinavia and Lapland, written for young readers. The catalog record names no author. Du Chaillu, the explorer famous for his African journeys and gorilla tales, here turns north, to the country where winter night lasts for weeks.

The narrative opens on the highroad skirting Sweden's southern coast, then turning north along the Baltic and the Gulf of Bothnia. Reindeer sledges, Sami camps, and the strange light of the polar night fill the journey. Du Chaillu writes with his usual gusto, mixing natural history with personal peril. The book fed the era's appetite for far places, and it still carries the chill and wonder of the Arctic dark.
22997-second-sight:
Lambertson will not talk in Second Sight, a story of unwanted knowledge. The narrator can read him and find out, he reflects, but suspects he is not supposed to know yet. Lambertson did not even mention he was back, though the narrator knew he would catch him five miles down the road. Distance, he notes, makes little difference any more, if he just ignores it.

A gift like that isolates its owner, and the story leans into the loneliness. Knowing what others hide sounds like power until it arrives uninvited. The telling stays low-key and troubled rather than flashy. Readers get a thoughtful piece of speculative fiction about perception, privacy, and the burden of seeing farther than your neighbors can.
23233-posthumous-works-of-the-author-of-:
The Posthumous Works gather writings left behind by the author of A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Mary Wollstonecraft. In notes quoted here, she judges her own draft honestly. Some incidents, she says, ought to be moved and given stronger shading, and she wished to use criticism before shaping her outline into a story.

Only a few friends saw that manuscript in her lifetime. The volume lets readers meet a major writer mid-revision, weighing how true events should be reordered and heightened for fiction. It is valuable both for the unfinished work itself and for the rare view of her craft.
a-thief-in-the-night: A Thief in the Night, E, w, hornung's raffles stories, the night thief. This book preserves that collection. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. Later readers can locate it. Those who study the era will use it in their work.
aslauga-s-knight: A knight serves his lady through hard trials in Fouqué’s old tale. He keeps his vows through arms and woe. A sweet, brave love story in knightly dress. Chivalry at its most tender and true.
burning-daylight: Jack London's 1910 novel about "Burning Daylight" Harnish, a Klondike king who conquers the gold fields with sheer nerve, then tries to conquer New York finance and nearly loses his soul. Part adventure, part love story, part warning about money, it is London's most autobiographical novel and one of his most readable.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-conrad-of-utr: A 1913 entry on Conrad of Utrecht — a bishop of the Dutch see. Michael Ott records his career. The entry preserves his modest fame. His see served the medieval age. A prelate of the eleventh century. His St. Mary's church is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lamprecht: This 1913 reference article on Lamprecht — the Alexander singer. Arthur F.J. Remy honors his famous Alexanderlied. His verse sang the Macedonian's deeds. Germany loved the martial muse. The twelfth century knew his name. His 1170 death is famed. His 1170 Alexander is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-monastery-of-: Tallaght was the great Irish monastery of the Culdees, the ascetic reformers of the 700s and 800s. This entry covers its foundation, its rule, and its scholars. The stern school of Irish monasticism: its rule demanded the strictest asceticism of early Ireland.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-right: Right is the moral power over what is one's due. This long entry examines its kinds, its foundation, and its philosophy. The just claim of the person: its deep root lies in nature's law of God the Maker of all.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-gregory-of: St. Gregory of Utrecht was the abbot of the Frisian mission. This entry traces his Boniface, his school, and his fame. The master of the Dutch clergy: his famed school crowned Utrecht in the 750s' Frisia in the north of the mission.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-spanish-b: The bull-fight is the Spanish spectacle. This entry examines its toreros, its danger, and its morality. The corrida of the Iberian arenas: their brave bulls crowned Seville in the 1700s of the arenas in the truly very old busy Maestranza.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-dwight: Dwight was the anatomist of Harvard. This entry traces his 1800s, his Boston, and his fame. The physician of the American schools: his famed Boston crowned Harvard in the 1870s of the Holmes in the truly very old brick school.
children-of-the-night: Robinson's 1897 Children of the Night gathers dark New England verse. Gloom broods. The Tower library holds the full text. It childed night. Poems darkened. Yankees mused. Shadows fell. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
doe-osti-3006359-the-effect-of-luminance: Nighttime glare got luminance-patterned, and this DOE CRADA final covers discomfort response. The pages detail the findings. The lighting folks get their closeout. The pattern was luminance. The closeout was lighting. The response was discomfort. The report was CRADA.
doe-osti-3012213-resistive-wall-simulati: DARHT walls got resistively simulated, and this DOE text covers the multi-pulse line. The pages detail the findings. The accelerator folks get their data. The walls were resistive. The data were accelerator. The line was multi-pulse. The simulations were wall.
her-prairie-knight: A B. M. Bower Western romance about a prairie girl and her cowboy knight. Cattle country, chivalry, and love in the author's authentic style. Charming frontier fiction from a master of the genre. Bower's cowboys are the real thing, drawn from life on the Montana range.
light:
Henri Barbusse wrote this novel, translated by Fitzwater Wray in 1919. Barbusse had already won fame as author of Under Fire. Twenty-three chapters run from Myself through Face to Face. Titles like The Storm, The Ruins, and Ghosts mark the route.

The narrator opens at his desk as the evening clock strikes seven. All his weekdays feel alike from beginning to end. Marie, brawlers, and apparitions disturb that dull routine. The closing chapters move toward the light of the title. Chapters named A Summary and The Brawler interrupt the quiet. De Profundis Clamavi and Eyes That See mark the spiritual turn.
literary-copyright:
Charles Dudley Warner addresses literary copyright in this piece. The text opens at the National Institute of Arts and Letters. That body held its first public meeting under discussion here. Members came by invitation from the American Social Science Association.

At Saratoga Springs in September 1899, members voted for independence. They adopted a revised constitution agreed upon in New York. The institute's object is advancing art and literature, Warner explains. Membership requires notable achievement in art or letters. Active membership would probably settle near one hundred, Warner reports. Honorary and associate members could join without numerical limit.
love-at-second-sight:
Love at Second Sight is a society novel by Ada Leverson, first published in 1916. It is book three of her Little Ottleys series. The story opens with a crash, shrieks, and a quarrel on a staircase. Edith Ottley rises from her blue sofa to find her son Archie blaming Madame Frabelle.

Archie is a calm boy of ten with sly humor in his glance. Around Edith's home moves the world of London drawing rooms. Visits, guests, and love affairs fill Leverson's light, witty pages. She writes of marriage and manners with a gentle sting. The novel charms readers who like quiet comedy of society.
midnight:
Octavus Roy Cohen published this detective novel in 1921. Cohen was already known for The Crimson Alibi and Gray Dusk. The story begins out of a storm, with a suit-case that must be opened. A chapter heading gives the detective's rule: find the woman.

The investigator Carroll interviews visitors, a valet, and several women tied to the case. Hazel Gresham, Evelyn Rogers, and Roland Warren all enter the inquiry. Later chapters return to the suit-case, a woman in a taxi, and a suspect with no alibi. Cohen builds a period mystery of clues, accusations, and loose ends.
nasa-tm-19650003087-pressure-measurement:
Earl R Keener, at the High-Speed Flight Station at Edwards in California, reported flight pressure readings for a delta wing in October 1959. The wing was conically cambered, meaning its surface was curved in a cone-like way. The aircraft was the F-102A, and speeds were transonic, near the speed of sound.

Keener presents pressures measured in real flight, not in a tunnel. Flight data check whether tunnel results hold on a real aircraft. For a cambered delta wing, those readings matter for lift and control. The report preserves that measured record.
nasa-tm-19670026211-preliminary-results-:
C. Catoe, W. Nordberg, P. Thaddeus, and G. Ling, of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center, wrote this report in August 1967. It gives early results from aircraft flight tests of an electrically scanning microwave radiometer. The instrument was designed for a meteorological satellite, and scanning its beam electronically, with no moving antenna, promised a sturdier sensor.

Flown on NASA's Convair 990 aircraft, the radiometer proved that satellite radiation measurements could extend from the infrared into much longer microwave wavelengths. Its phased-array antenna swept a narrow beam sideways across the flight path, building two-dimensional maps of Earth's brightness temperature. Flights crossed Arctic Ocean ice, Alaskan tundra and snow, southwestern deserts, midwestern farmland, Yucatan forests, and storms over land and water. Preliminary displays showed the instrument performing as expected. Land-water and ice contrasts mapped clearly under all cloud conditions, and ocean storm activity could be identified positively.
nasa-tm-19670028348-synthesis-of-ultrahi:
Li-Chen Hsu, of NASA's Lewis Research Center in Cleveland, presented this paper at a polymers meeting in Cleveland, Ohio, in April 1967. It covers the making of poly(ethylene terephthalate), the plastic called PET, with very long molecule chains. Such ultrahigh molecular weight material was wanted to test how chain length affects PET's behavior at cryogenic temperatures, where aerospace uses were in view.

Hsu prepared PET with an average molecular weight on the order of one hundred twenty thousand, starting from commercial grade material. The reaction ran in the solid state inside a gas chromatograph apparatus, an unusual piece of equipment for polymer synthesis. Parameters studied included the catalyst, particle size, and the molecular weight of the starting material. Reaction temperature and time mattered, as did the nature and flow rate of the carrier gas sweeping through the apparatus.
nasa-tm-19690018398-sounding-rocket-para:
Brian C. Pierman, of Goddard Space Flight Center's Flight Program Office, prepared this March 1969 report, X-326-69-162, on sounding rocket parameters versus flight reliability. He compares two physical parameters, flight weight and telemetry channel count, against flight failure rates. The purpose is practical: choosing which environmental tests sounding rocket payloads should have to pass before flying.

A clear correlation is established between greater weight and decreased flight success, Pierman reports. No correlation is established between telemetry channels and flight success. Charts track failure percentages for Apache and Aerobee rockets across moving weight brackets. The finding gives test planners a simple rule: heavier payloads deserve the closer look, while channel count alone signals nothing.
now-or-never-or-the-adventures-of-bobby-:
Oliver Optic wrote Now or Never, or the Adventures of Bobby Bright, as a story for young folks. William T. Adams, his real name, entered it in Massachusetts in 1856. This new edition came from the Mershon Company in New York, under an 1884 copyright. The book is dedicated to his nephew, Charles Henry Pope.

A front picture shows Bobby declaring he is big enough to protect his mother, and will do it. That line, from page forty-two, sets the hero's stamp. Optic wrote boys who work, save, and stand up at home. Young America of his day read such tales for both fun and example. Bobby's adventures test a poor boy's grit.
raabe-german-moonlight:
Moonlight falls on small-town Germany in Wilhelm Raabe's novella German Moonlight, presented here in English. Ordinary people carry inner lives far richer than their quiet streets suggest. Raabe, often called the German Dickens, specialized in exactly that discovery, and this tale shows his method at its gentlest.

Warm humor and quiet melancholy share the telling, as old memories stir under the moon's calm light. Nothing sensational happens; everything human does. Raabe trusted readers to find depth without being shouted at. The novella makes a gentle, moonlit entry into his large and rewarding body of work. Those who enjoy it will find a whole shelf of his fiction waiting in both languages.
the-boy-knight: The Boy Knight, G, a, henty's crusades tale, the young crusader. This book preserves that adventure. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. It awaits future readers. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
the-city-of-dreadful-night: James Thomson's 1874 poem of urban despair: a night-walk through a London of fog, hopelessness, and lost faith. In somber, powerful verse, Thomson made the modern city a symbol of spiritual desolation. The great Victorian poem of pessimism, admired by all who know it.
the-secret-of-the-night: The Secret of the Night, Gaston Leroux's Russian mystery. The night's secret. This book preserves that novel. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
the-tavern-knight: The Tavern Knight, Rafael Sabatini's novel of the English Civil War. Its tale unfolds. This book preserves that historical romance. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care.
twelfth-night: Shakespeare's perfect romantic comedy: shipwrecked Viola disguises herself as a boy, loves her master, and is loved by the countess he adores. Add the drunk Sir Toby, the prig Malvolio, and Feste's songs, and you have the best-loved comedy in English. Joyful, musical, and wise about love's confusions.
